title: The horde gathers
body: In the forty seconds before a boss arrives, creatures come faster and faster, up to one and a half times the pace.

title: The horde falters
body: For about twenty seconds after a boss falls, creatures come at a third of the pace, then ease back. A breath to feel what you just became.

title: The night deepens
body: Once each of the first four bosses' lulls is over, creature health steps up, easing in over a minute, and the Watch tells you when. It deepens only as far as you can take it: if the last minute and a half has been draining you, or brought you low, the step is smaller or does not come at all, and the Watch says so: The night deepens, deepens a little, or holds back.

title: The deep night pays
body: The deeper you let it go, the richer the next reliquary: after a full step, three gifts are twice as likely and five three times. Every step you take adds to the night's score, up to a fifth more over a whole night.

title: Built to take hits
body: What counts is the health the night drains from you, not how often it hits you. A thorns or lifesteal build that stands in the crowd and heals every blow back is doing fine, and the night treats it that way.

title: No flat walk to dawn
body: Once a battlefield's last wave of creatures has arrived, the pace keeps climbing, up to about 80% by dawn, as far as the last deepening went. A build that has run away with the night no longer walks to dawn.

title: Reliquaries
body: A boss used to leave gold and a handful of gems. With Tides armed, it also leaves a violet reliquary where it fell. A reliquary holds one gift, three gifts one time in five, or five gifts one time in twenty. Fortune improves the odds. Each gift is a step down the road your build is already on, taken in this order:
A brimming reliquary can take a weapon from rank 7 to evolved in one touch. That is the chase: good luck at a boss can carry you ahead for a long stretch, and a stingy one leaves you to earn it.
list: An evolution that is ready. A weapon at rank 8 with its passive learned evolves on the spot.
The passive a finished weapon is waiting on. Rank 8 but missing its pairing? You learn it.
A rank on the weapon nearest its evolution.

title: Velocity
body: Speed alone reaches the same creatures a little sooner. At its cap it was worth −12% to +3% to most weapons, and it made a herd or a seeking bolt worse. Every rank now also makes projectiles hit 7.5% harder. The card and the damage shown on your weapons say so.

title: Expanse on Gale Chakram
body: Area threw the ring further, so it turned past the crowd and spent the extra flight on empty ground. It made an evolved chakram 21% weaker. The ring now widens as it reaches further.

title: Shadowflame
body: Each burst marked the creatures it touched as already struck. An evolved Umbral Bolt passes through everything, so it skipped them and lost full hits to smaller bursts. Once a bolt passes through everything, the flame now burns inside it instead.

title: Truestrike
body: Homing bent a spread of arrows onto one target, which was slightly worse against a crowd until the volley evolved. The arrows now also strike harder.

title: Moonlit Herd
body: The extra beast and the moonburst mattered early and faded to almost nothing. The herd now runs harder too.

title: Radiant Gyre
body: The pulse is worth plenty early and little once the gyre evolves. The blades now bite harder too.

title: Hallowed Hands
body: Mostly a mend, but the wider ground now reaches further.

sec: Every weapon, on the damage meter
title: Skybreak
body: Thirty jumps with almost no falloff meant one cast cleared the screen. It now jumps fourteen times and loses more with each. Arcweb starts lower and grows more with every rank.

sec: Every weapon, on the damage meter
title: Reckoning and Mote Cascade
body: Discs that bounce through a crowd, and motes that seek it out, reach everything first. Both come down once evolved; their damage to bosses stays.

sec: Every weapon, on the damage meter
title: The weapons at your side
body: Rend and Mend, Circle of Dawn, Gyrestorm, Temple Breaker and Verdant Gaze were last on every meter. Each now hits much harder in company, and no harder on a boss.

Each weapon's share of what the five weapons in its build did, in sixty random builds, averaged over the four ways of playing, on the Pale Wastes at Professional. A fair share is 20%. Evolved, every weapon now takes 18% to 22%; at rank 5, 18% to 21%; at rank 3, 16% to 26%. Full nights played by the bot on the same seeds reach dawn about as often as before.

title: DZ, the Graveblade
body: Across four battlefields at Professional he reached dawn 3 times in 8 and fell soonest of anyone. More health, and more mending, which Blood Rite also turns into damage.

title: Standing stones wait for you
body: On Highmoor, a shrine no longer sinks while you are inside charging it. It goes once you step out after its time is up. Its ring now shows the time it has left, the way Beans does.

title: Beans says what you bought
body: Buying eggs puts a word over her head: how many, and the damage and health they gave.

title: The night has light
body: The field now darkens toward midnight and warms toward dawn, in each battlefield's own colour. You stand in the watch fire's glow, every spell lights and tints the ground it crosses, danger glows red, the brightest magic blooms, and mist, fireflies, dust, snow, wisps or drizzle move through the air. Balanced quality keeps the light and skips the bloom.

title: The night has a pulse
body: The score used to sound the same in a full field as an empty one. As the night gets dangerous, a second band now comes in under each battlefield's music: a kick, a backbeat on that battlefield's own drum, a shaker and a bass line walking the chords. It is all there by the time things are really bad, and it goes as the danger does. The melody gets an echo of its own, the music darkens toward midnight, and in the last stretch before dawn a high bell comes in over it.

title: You can hear what you hit with
body: Every weapon landed with the same blow. Now the blow carries its school: fire hisses, frost clinks, arcane fizzes, holy rings, nature knocks, shadow thuds and steel rings off. An elite goes down with a crunch and a low ring, not the same thud as the crowd, and a boss falls with a great bell and a chord rising over it. Beans rings her cart bell when she sets up, says hello, and rolls away when she packs up.

title: Wolves hunt, ghouls guard
body: Spirit wolves and ghouls were one creature with different numbers. Now they do different jobs. Spirit wolves run as a pack: when a boss, an elite or something that shoots is in reach they all go for it, each bite harder for every packmate already on it, and a pounce mauls what is around it. Ghouls stay close and turn on whatever is nearest you; their claws slow what they rake and leave it rotting, taking more damage from everything, your weapons included, for a few seconds. Rotting creatures shed green motes.
chips: wolves on a boss 5x the ghouls

title: Every calling has its passive
body: The Graveblade, the Ruinseeker, the Druid and the Monk each had an epic passive that deepened their power. The other eight callings now do too, offered once you hold the calling: Undertow (Spellflood), Hallowed Mending (Radiant Barrier), Ruthless (Opportunist), Stalker's Patience (The Quarry), Slow Burn (Seething Blood), Bountiful Tithe (Reaper's Tithe), Deep Roots (Waystones) and Fervor (Conviction).

Four of them also work without their calling, the way Curdled Light works without Blood Rite, and are offered to a build that can use them. Undertow: gathering gems cuts the wait of your slowest weapon (with Greed's Pull). Hallowed Mending: overheal becomes a small Ward that takes hits first (with any healing). Ruthless: a crit finishes an ordinary creature left low (with Precision). Slow Burn: every blow you take Smoulders into extra damage (with Thorns or Ironhide). The card shows whichever half you would get.

title: The meter's share, lit
body: The percentage on each damage and healing meter row is bold and tinted to its source, like the name and figure beside it.

title: Ruin Unbound
body: Every union was balanced with no passives taken, and that is where Ruin Unbound hid. It fired two seeking, piercing, splashing bolts, so each rank of Duplicity added half again, where the median weapon gains about a tenth. Velocity and Expanse stacked on top. With every passive at its cap it took 45% of a build's damage. It now fires three lighter bolts: the same union without passives, and a third less for every bolt Duplicity adds.

title: Hallowed Ground and Blighted Earth, layered
body: Ground that heals paid out once per layer: every zone you stood in healed you on its own. Haste and above all Perennial make zones overlap, so with every passive Hallowed Ground healed 153 a second where Grave Tether healed 96. Now, standing on several layers of the same ground heals you once, at the best layer. The heal on each is raised so that without those passives both mend exactly what they did.
chips: Hallowed Ground, every passive 153 → 80 a second

title: Boil Over and the Spring actually mend
body: Health is kept in whole points, and every heal was rounded down. A heal that trickles in every frame, like Boil Over's 3% a second or the Spring's pools, is a fraction of a point each frame, so it rounded to nothing, every frame, and never healed at all. The fraction now carries over to the next frame.

title: The Masked Admiral, ashore
body: Sink the Dust Galleon and the Admiral fights you on foot. That duel is the climax of the Dustreach finale, and it was the softer half of it: a little less health than the ship, one small target every weapon reaches, over in about a minute. She now has twice the health. The ship is unchanged.

title: The barrier and the Ward build back
body: Radiant Barrier and Hallowed Mending's Ward were fed only by healing, and every blow they soaked held that off again. In a crowd with light healing the barrier averaged 3% full and the Ward 1%: a sliver that broke as it formed. Now, once broken, either one builds back on its own over about 4 seconds. No blow can stop that, every heal you take hurries it, and it comes back at half its full size. The HUD shows it re-forming. Healing still tops it up from there.
chips: barrier, light healing 3% → 25% full on average

title: A second job costs damage
body: A weapon that heals you, or slows what it hits, and deals as much as one that only deals damage is simply better. Grave Tether and Blightfield were taking more than a fair share of the damage while healing best of all. Now the weapons with a second job sit below the pure-damage ones, and the balance tests check it: healers at about four fifths of their damage, weapons that slow at a little over nine tenths. Measured in the real waves with every passive at its cap, 120 builds of five.

title: Skybreak, Moonbrand; Knifestorm and Axe Gyre up
body: Skybreak topped the meter in 12 of the 28 builds it was in; now 3. Moonbrand came down with it. Knifestorm and Axe Gyre, the two lowest, came up. Every pure-damage weapon now takes 19% to 23% of a five-weapon build.

title: Stormcall
body: It ate Skybreak and Gyrestorm and was flat worse than them: 61% of their damage. A union is allowed to be a little less than the pair, since it frees a slot, but not that much less. Its blades circle close, where Skybreak had reached far out, so it gets reach back through its own lightning: more blades, and more of its cuts call the storm.

title: Sanctuary
body: With every passive at its cap, Sanctuary took 56% of a build's damage. It is not the strongest union (it is below the middle against a crowd that cannot die, and weak on a boss), but at full Expanse its ring covers the ground the horde stands on, so it took almost every kill. It now pulses less often, a little narrower. Its healing a second and its damage to a boss are kept where they were.

title: Axe Gyre, Arcweb and Judgement Disc
body: A new sweep flagged these three: Axe Gyre gaining nearly five times its damage from Expanse, and Arcweb and Judgement Disc far behind. Both readings came from a field of creatures that never die. In the real waves, with every passive at its cap, all three take between 18% and 23% of a five-weapon build, where a fair share is 20%. They are unchanged.

title: Storm of Steel and Truestrike, on a boss
body: Ring weapons hit a boss harder because most of a ring flies past it. Truestrike, carried into Storm of Steel, made every knife seek, so none flew past, and all fifteen landed at the full bonus: ten times what the union did to a boss before. A shot that seeks only because of a discovery now keeps no boss bonus above normal. Volley with Truestrike is affected the same way, less sharply.
chips: Storm of Steel on a boss 46k → 8.4k a second

title: Wolves and ghouls, drawn at last
body: Your summons were their card icons, lit and bobbing about the field. Now they are creatures. Spirit wolves gallop on real legs, pale fire with a hot core, their paws thinning into mist, a ghost of each one streaming behind it and motes of its light lifting off its back. A pounce lands as jaws snapping shut on the thing, and whatever the pack is hunting wears its mark, a turning ring. Ghouls are hunched grave-corpses with rot glowing through the hide and at the rim of the body, dragging their knuckles in a pool of it, dripping from the claws. Their rake sweeps a visible arc exactly as wide as what it hits.

title: Ghouls break loose
body: A strong build kills everything before it reaches a ghoul's short leash, and a tester's ghouls never touched anything. Now a ghoul that has raked nothing for 4 seconds, while there is a crowd further out, runs to the thickest of it and bursts: rot over a wide circle, six rakes' worth of damage, everything it touches left rotting longer. They go one at a time: when one breaks loose, the others start their wait again, so a pack of ghouls sends one out every 4 seconds rather than all at once. It rises again at your side 6 seconds later, clawing up out of the ground, and a small ring by you counts it back. A ghoul with work at your side never leaves it: a breakout is half what a working guard does.

title: Card numbers stay in their columns
body: A weapon card's numbers sit in two columns, and a row a few pixels too wide for its half (Duration on Axe Gyre or Thornbloom) took the whole width, its figure pushed to the far edge. The arrow's spacing now closes up first, then the numbers set a size smaller, and only then does a row span the card.

title: The blow that ended it
body: The defeat screen says what got through, when, and how hard it hit: "Mossback Stonehide got through at 28:30, and they hit you for 246. 66.6k creatures did not make it to dawn."

title: Waystones are built, not handed out
body: A stone rose every three seconds, ember, spring, gale, over and over, whatever you did. Now each stone is built by a way of fighting and rises where you stand when it is full. The Ember fills from damage you deal close to you, and erupts as it comes up before it burns everything near it. The Spring fills from healing, overheal included, and rains pools around you: step into one to mend. The Gale fills from ground you cover, and near it your weapons fire faster. A brawler raises embers, a healer springs, a kiter gales. Each has its own bar on the HUD, and stones of different kinds stack their effects. Measured at Professional against the old stones, the calling is worth the same; it is just yours to steer now.

title: What Thorns ranks do
body: The Thorns card said only that attackers take damage back. It now says how much: every rank returns another 10 plus 60% of the blow, so rank 5 sends back 50 plus three times what hit you.

title: You can see what heals
body: Cards for anything that heals you, a weapon, a passive or a blessing, carry a small green plus on their mark.

title: The build sheet, reordered
body: Your blessings now sit above the build: beside the tabs on the pause screen, and under the Watch's log on the results screen, where your eye lands first and there was empty space. Passives run four across and discoveries three where there is room, so less scrolling. The damage and healing meters are bars in each source's own colour, with its mark, a bright name and a bold figure, instead of a faint green wash.

title: The run graph is back on the results screen
body: A Show graph button on the results banner swaps the run's figures for its timeline (damage dealt and taken a second, across the whole run) and Show figures swaps them back. The banner keeps its size either way, and the next run's results open on whichever you chose last.

title: The banish hint where you look
body: "Pick a card to banish it from this run" sat at the far right edge of the screen. It is now centred between the Reroll and Banish buttons and the cards, and a size larger, and the cards have not moved.

title: A beating is easier on the ears
body: A tank build takes a hit every time its grace runs out, and every one was the same full-weight grunt. Now each blow you take within a few seconds of the last comes in a little quieter, settling about a third lower under a steady beating, and a few seconds of peace brings it back. A heavy blow, one that takes a real share of your health, is always heard in full.

title: Adaptive quality
body: Dynamic resolution is now Adaptive quality. When a fight gets too heavy for your machine, it drops the bloom first, then the mist, then the night lighting, and only then draws at a lower resolution. It keeps each step only if frames actually got faster, and everything comes back at the start of your next run. On a machine with no graphics card this took the heaviest fight from about 55 ms a frame to about 33, with the night lighting kept.

title: The mix, rebalanced
body: Measured off real nights, the music sat 12 to 16 dB under the effects in every fight, so under a wall of hits it was not quiet, it was gone. It comes up, the hit chatter comes down a little, and the whole game is louder: it used about a quarter of the level it could, so most players had their volume turned right up to make up for it. You may want to turn your volume down a notch.

title: Beans follows the bosses
body: She came on a clock of her own, which put her at 30:30 and brought her back to the breather just after she had taken your coin. Now she sets up just after a boss falls, while its gold is on the ground, skips the last boss before the finale, keeps her breather visit and packs up when the fight begins. Her timer says which boss she is waiting on.

title: Ranks at a glance
body: Level-up cards show a rank as a row of ticks instead of "Rank 6 to 7": solid for the ranks you have, dim for the one the card gives, empty for the rest. The card under your cursor flickers its new tick on. The line it frees goes to the weapon's numbers, and a number too long for half the card takes the whole width.

title: Fields keep their art
body: With more than four fields on the ground every one of them turned into a plain ring. Now the newest field of each weapon keeps its runes, mire or brambles, however busy the ground gets.

title: The Nightly is random again
body: The Nightly drew its survivor, battlefield and oath from the date, and dates next to each other drew almost the same thing, so Abbot Eisen came up night after night. The draw is now well mixed: over a year every survivor comes up about as often as any other. Today's Nightly changes.

title: What Velocity shows
body: The damage on your weapon cards and the pause sheet now includes Velocity's harder hits.

Every weapon at 1:00, 5:00, 9:00, 14:00 and 20:00 with a stage's worth of passives; every weapon with each damage passive at nothing and at its cap; every discovery on and off at each stage; every weapon against the real waves at 9:00 and 20:00; and sixty random builds of five at 5:00, 9:00 and 20:00, circling close or keeping away, with every passive or a few, for each weapon's share of the meter. A weapon that seemed to lead full nights was replayed in the same builds with another in its place. Then full nights played by the bot on every battlefield at Professional, every survivor, the same seeds with Tides off and on, recorded every ten seconds: how much health went, how low it got, and how many creatures stood within reach. The previous patch notes are here.

title: Wolves and ghouls, brought to heel
body: Three wolves or three ghouls did four to five times a weapon's damage at 5:00 and over twice at 9:00, then fell behind by 20:00. Their early power was kills, not damage: a bite or a maul finishes trash whatever it hits for, so softer bites barely moved them.

So they come slower and hit harder later. Bites come every 0.85s, not 0.55s, and a bite grows with your level alone, with no flat base. The wolves' maul around the quarry is lighter and narrower, and a wolf waits longer before the next bite after a kill. Ghouls rake less often, over a slightly smaller sweep. The pack bonus on a shared quarry, mostly bosses and elites, doubles.

title: Tether of Anguish, a panic heal
body: Evolved, the tether mended about 59 health a second from range once a line of creatures formed, and kiting with it was close to immortality.
Now it mends in full at half health or below, and less the healthier you are: about a third at full. The rest counts as overheal, so Curdled Light still feeds on it.

title: Ruthless ranks matter
body: Taken without Opportunist, Ruthless finished an ordinary creature a crit left under 3% health a rank. Late on a crit kills trash anyway, so ranks two to five did close to nothing.
Now the execute is a flat 6% from rank 1, and every rank makes your crits land 8% harder on anything below 35% health, elites and bosses included.

title: The healers, evolved
body: Counted by what actually landed, evolved Rend and Mend still took more of the meter than any weapon that only does damage, and it heals as well. So did Dawnpulse and Hallowed Ring, a little. Their evolved damage comes down until they sit where a weapon that also heals should; against bosses they stay where they were.
Testers also pointed at evolved Arcweb. Counted the same way, it sits a little under its fair share, so it stays as it is.

title: Bombs and hourglasses don't feed themselves
body: A bomb's own kills could roll more bombs and hourglasses, and so could creatures killed while time was stopped. A luck build once chained 74 charges and 46 hourglasses in one night.

Those kills no longer roll them, and none drop while the tide crests before a boss. And each one needs a moment to come back: right after a bomb drops, the next bomb's chance starts at nothing and climbs back over about twenty seconds (twenty-five for an hourglass). Every kill is still a roll, so the gaps are still luck, but a lucky build late in the night now gets one roughly every fifteen to twenty-five seconds instead of a constant shower. Early nights are unchanged; potions and gold are untouched.

title: The meter counts what landed
body: A blow that kills counted its whole size on the damage meter, not the health it actually took, so big hits and screen-clears looked stronger than they were. The meter now counts only what landed. Overkill and healing sit behind two buttons under the meter: hover them to see each source's share.
A ghoul's rot gets its own line, so the extra damage it lends your weapons is no longer counted as theirs.

title: Run codes
body: The end of every night has a Copy run code button: one line of text holding the night as it went, every card offered and taken, where you moved, what hit what and what dropped. Paste it to us and we can read the night back for balance.

title: Healing, bosses, unions and banishes, shown
body: The survivor card and build sheet show healing received. Bosses are drawn over the spell light again, so you never lose one in your own effects. A union's tooltip lists the discoveries it carries from both weapons and what each does. What you have banished is listed on the pause sheet and the Banish button.

title: Death keeps coming, and you can kill him
body: Staying for Death used to be a coin toss: one touch either killed you outright or never landed. Now overtime costs hits. Death's touch takes a share of your health, 30% at first and 5% more every minute. He comes back sooner as the minutes pass, and more of him can be on the field at once.

And he blinks. A pale ring opens where you are running; less than a second later he is standing in it. Turn and you are clear. Run straight and it costs you a fifth of your health or more, and your healing withers to half for a few seconds.
He is still killable. Every Death you put down is announced with the night's count, and it goes on the end screen and in your records.
chips: touch 30% of your health, +5% a minute

title: Dread Command is a weapon
body: Wolves and ghouls now need a weapon slot. Dread Command, which used to be a passive, is the summoner's weapon. Its own sigil marks the thick of the crowd and sends every summon at it at once, and every rank drives them harder and faster.

Spirit Companion and Grave Call are only offered while you hold it. Evolved with Might it becomes The Dread Host: summons strike three and a half times as hard and a third again as often, and the sigil falls twice as often with every summon's next bite ready.
chips: each rank +4% summon damage, +2% speed; evolved +250%

title: Curdled Light keeps up
body: Curdled Light was a build at 9:00 and an afterthought by 20:00, because its pulse never grew with you and erupted at your feet, where nothing lived late in a night.

Now it grows with your Might and with your arsenal, more for every rank and far more for every evolved weapon. And it erupts on the nearest of the crowd instead of around you. A committed Curdled build is now worth a bit over half a weapon all night long.

title: Skybreak stays
body: Testers felt evolved Arcweb took kills that belonged to their other weapons. We tested it as the first weapon to evolve, beside weapons at rank 3 and at rank 6, and with all five evolved: it came out at or below its fair share every time. Sending its hops past what is at your feet changed nothing, so it stays as it is.
Part of what you saw was the meter: it used to credit a killing blow with its full size. It now counts only what landed. If it still looks greedy, send us the run code.

title: The last stretch thickens
body: Without Tides, the back half of a night went flat. Now, once the last phase begins, the horde keeps growing - more to kill, not tougher - to about two-fifths more by dawn. Tides nights keep their own steeper rise.

title: Knifestorm and Axe Gyre, evolved
body: With the healers brought down, Knifestorm and Axe Gyre picked up what they gave up and ran over a fair share. Their evolved damage comes down a little; against bosses they stay where they were.
